## Proof

**Answer: Yes, the statement is correct.** The zero element $0_p \in E_p$ is precisely the equivalence class $[(p,0)]$, and this is well-defined precisely because the transition maps $g_{ij}(p)$ are linear (in fact invertible linear) maps.

---

### Setup and interpretation

In the standard cocycle construction of a vector bundle, the transition maps are
$$g_{ij}: U_i \cap U_j \to \mathrm{GL}(r,\mathbb{R}),$$
satisfying the cocycle conditions
$$g_{ii}(p)=\mathrm{id},\qquad g_{ij}(p)\,g_{jk}(p)=g_{ik}(p)\quad\text{on }U_i\cap U_j\cap U_k.$$
(The notation $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to\mathbb{R}^r$ in the statement is the usual shorthand for "to $\mathrm{GL}(r,\mathbb{R})\subset\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}$"; the cocycle condition forces each $g_{ij}(p)$ to be invertible, since $g_{ij}(p)g_{ji}(p)=\mathrm{id}$.)

The total space is $E=\bigsqcup_i U_i\times\mathbb{R}^r/\sim$ with
$$(p,\lambda)_i \sim (q,\mu)_j \iff p=q\in U_i\cap U_j \text{ and } \lambda = g_{ij}(p)\,\mu.$$

The fiber $E_p$ is the set of equivalence classes of pairs whose first component is $p$.

---

### Step 1. The class $[(p,0)]$ is independent of the chart.

Fix $p\in X$ and pick any two indices $i,j$ with $p\in U_i\cap U_j$. We must show that the representative $(p,0)_i\in U_i\times\mathbb{R}^r$ and the representative $(p,0)_j\in U_j\times\mathbb{R}^r$ define the same equivalence class, i.e. $(p,0)_i\sim(p,0)_j$.

By definition of $\sim$, this requires $0 = g_{ij}(p)\cdot 0$. Since $g_{ij}(p)\in\mathrm{GL}(r,\mathbb{R})$ is a **linear** map, $g_{ij}(p)\cdot 0 = 0$. Hence
$$(p,0)_i \sim (p,0)_j.$$

So the class $[(p,0)]\in E_p$ is well-defined regardless of which chart $U_i\ni p$ we use to represent it. (If $p$ lies only in $U_i$, there is nothing to check.)

---

### Step 2. $[(p,0)]$ is the additive identity of $E_p$.

The vector-space structure on $E_p$ is defined chart-wise: for $[(p,\lambda)],[(p,\mu)]\in E_p$ represented in the same chart $U_i$,
$$[(p,\lambda)] + [(p,\mu)] := [(p,\lambda+\mu)]_i,\qquad c\cdot[(p,\lambda)] := [(p,c\lambda)]_i.$$

This is well-defined because each transition map $g_{ij}(p)$ is linear: if we switch representatives via $\lambda'=g_{ij}(p)\lambda$, $\mu'=g_{ij}(p)\mu$, then
$$\lambda'+\mu' = g_{ij}(p)(\lambda+\mu),\qquad c\lambda' = g_{ij}(p)(c\lambda),$$
so the sum and scalar multiple transform consistently under $\sim$.

Now for any $[(p,\lambda)]\in E_p$, represented in any chart $U_i\ni p$,
$$[(p,\lambda)] + [(p,0)] = [(p,\lambda+0)]_i = [(p,\lambda)].$$
Because the addition is well-defined (Step 1 guarantees $[(p,0)]$ is the same element no matter which chart represents it), this shows $[(p,0)]$ is a two-sided additive identity in $E_p$.

---

### Step 3. Local triviality confirms the identification.

Local triviality gives, for each $i$, a bundle chart $\varphi_i:\pi^{-1}(U_i)\to U_i\times\mathbb{R}^r$ sending $[(p,\lambda)]\mapsto(p,\lambda)$. Under $\varphi_i$, the element $[(p,0)]$ maps to $(p,0)$, which is the zero of the trivial fiber $\{p\}\times\mathbb{R}^r$. Since bundle charts are linear isomorphisms on fibers, the zero of the trivialization is exactly the zero of $E_p$. The cocycle/linearity of transitions guarantees this identification is consistent across all charts (Step 1), so the zero is a globally well-defined element of $E_p$, not merely a chart-dependent artifact.

---

### Conclusion

The zero element $0_p\in E_p$ is exactly the equivalence class $[(p,0)]$. The key fact making this correct is the **linearity** of the transition maps $g_{ij}(p)$: it ensures (a) the class $[(p,0)]$ does not depend on the chosen chart, and (b) it acts as the additive identity under the chart-wise vector-space structure. Local triviality then confirms this is the canonical zero of the fiber. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
